Physics

 Home
OurBigBook.com Words: 1M Articles: 26k
Physics investigates matter, motion, and interactions by building mathematical models and testing their consequences against observations. A physical law supplies a relation; a model specifies the objects, conditions, and approximations used to apply it. Classical mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, and quantum mechanics organize different aspects of these investigations. Their usefulness comes from turning measurements into predictions that can be checked and refined.
Consider a simple pendulum: how does its oscillation period change when its length changes? For small amplitude, the ideal model gives T0​=2πℓ/g​, where g is gravitational acceleration. Taking g=9.81m/s2 as the model parameter, a one-metre pendulum has predicted period 2.0061s. Increasing its length to four metres gives 4.0121s: quadrupling the length doubles the period. The point mass cancels from the equation, so changing it alone does not change this model's answer.
The prediction identifies a mechanism and a way to challenge it. The small-angle approximation replaces sinθ by θ; the full ideal equation predicts a longer period at large amplitude. At 60∘, its period is about 1.07318T0​, already a 7.3% change. Measurements at such amplitudes can reveal the limit of the approximation, while appreciable drag requires a damped pendulum. These distinctions are developed in simple pendulum and dimensional analysis. The small-amplitude model is also derived in Ling, Sanny and Moebs, University Physics, pendulums.
Several different experiments can become one calculation. Nondimensionalization rewrites the pendulum equation using τ=tg/ℓ​, leaving d2θ/dτ2+sinθ=0. All lengths share that dimensionless equation; the amplitude remains a parameter. Similarly, conservation laws and symmetry reveal features that many models share. This is one source of the subject's beauty: a compact relation can organize a large range of phenomena.
The connection to evidence remains essential when a model is elegant. In his introductory lectures, Richard Feynman emphasizes testing proposed relations by experiment and using idealizations whose accuracy depends on the conditions. [ref] A discrepancy can motivate a better measurement, a better approximation, or a different physical model; the mathematical calculation and the empirical assessment are both part of the explanation.

Radiation therapy

Words: 289 Articles: 8
Nuclear medicine OurBigBook.com
Treatment through controlled deposition of ionizing absorbed dose. External beams and internal radiopharmaceuticals require different delivery and radiation dosimetry models.
Biologically effective dose (BED=Nd(1+d/(α/β)))
Words: 46
Radiation therapy OurBigBook.com
An effect-equivalent dose derived from the linear-quadratic radiobiology model, with a subscript often indicating the tissue's assumed α/β in gray. It is distinct from the physical total absorbed dose Nd. Increasing fraction size at fixed tumour BED can increase the normal-tissue BED when the latter has smaller α/β.
Linear-quadratic radiobiology model (−lnS=αd+βd2)
Words: 50
Radiation therapy OurBigBook.com
A model for surviving fraction S after radiation dose d. Independent fully repaired fractions add their logarithmic effects. For N equal fractions and no repopulation, dividing the total log kill by α gives the biologically effective dose Nd(1+d/(α/β)). Comparing tissue types requires their own parameters and the same stated repair assumptions.
Depth-dose curve
Words: 40
Radiation therapy OurBigBook.com
The variation of absorbed dose with depth for a specified beam, geometry and medium. A megavoltage photon beam has a secondary-electron buildup region followed by gradual dose reduction. A nearly monoenergetic proton beam instead exhibits a Bragg peak near the end of its range.
Treatment plan
Words: 30
Radiation therapy OurBigBook.com
A specified geometry, beam configuration and dose prescription intended to cover a target while limiting normal-tissue dose. Robustness to setup, motion and anatomy changes is part of assessing a plan.
Proton therapy
Words: 54 Articles: 1
Radiation therapy OurBigBook.com
Treatment using proton beams with controllable finite range and a Bragg peak. Potential normal-tissue sparing must be assessed against range uncertainty, motion and biological-effect uncertainties.
Range uncertainty
Words: 31
Proton therapy OurBigBook.com
Uncertainty in where a charged-particle beam stops because of material conversion, anatomy, motion or delivery errors. A steep distal dose gradient makes it particularly consequential for target coverage and nearby tissue.
Photon radiotherapy
Words: 53 Articles: 1
Radiation therapy OurBigBook.com
External-beam treatment using photons that create secondary charged particles in tissue. Megavoltage depth-dose curves usually show build-up followed by an extended fall-off and exit dose.
Intensity-modulated radiotherapy
Words: 28
Photon radiotherapy OurBigBook.com
Treatment using spatially varying beam fluence to shape the combined three-dimensional dose distribution. Improved target conformity may come with dose distributed through a larger volume at lower levels.

A pharmaceutical containing a radionuclide, with uptake and clearance chosen for imaging or treatment. Biological targeting and radioactive decay jointly determine its useful signal and tissue dose.

Words: 21

A diagnostic bone tracer combining technetium-99m with a diphosphonate carrier. Uptake reflects bone turnover and delivery, rather than a unique disease diagnosis.
Technetium-99m
Words: 21

A metastable nuclear isomer used in diagnostic tracers, with approximately six-hour half-life and 140keV imageable gamma rays. Its chemical carrier determines biological uptake.

Matter

Words: 44
Physics OurBigBook.com
Material constituents such as particles and their composites. In cosmology, the narrower phrase pressureless matter usually refers to nonrelativistic components whose rest energy dominates their random kinetic energy, giving negligible pressure and density proportional to the inverse cube of the scale factor. This usage distinguishes the matter contribution from relativistic radiation in cosmology and vacuum energy.

The reference radiation dose divided by the test radiation dose giving the same specified biological endpoint. It depends on radiation quality, tissue, endpoint and dose, rather than being an immutable particle constant.

A dosimetric condition in which the charged-particle energy entering a small region balances the corresponding energy leaving it. Under appropriate equilibrium conditions, photon collision kerma equals absorbed dose. It can fail near material boundaries or in the buildup region of a high-energy photon beam.

Cross section (physics, σ)

Words: 146 Articles: 2
Physics OurBigBook.com
An effective area describing the strength of a specified interaction. With an incident particle flux j and NT​ independent target particles, the ideal event rate for that channel is jNT​σ.

Unpolarized cross section (∣M∣2​=(2s1​+1)(2s2​+1)1​∑initial,final​∣M∣2)

Words: 66
Cross section (physics) OurBigBook.com
For uncorrelated incoming beams with equally populated spin states, the measured cross section averages over initial polarizations and sums over unobserved final polarizations. The displayed average applies to two massive incoming particles with spins s1​,s2​. It is distinct from a prepared-polarization channel and from the final-state identical-particle factor in a final-state phase-space integral. A polarization channel with an amplitude that grows faster than the others can reach a perturbative bound before the averaged quantity does.

Two-body scattering cross section (dΩdσ​=64π2s1​∣pi​∣∣kf​∣​∣M∣2​)

Words: 52
Cross section (physics) OurBigBook.com
For distinguishable final particles, the centre-of-momentum frame cross section is the displayed product of the invariant amplitude, incoming flux and relativistic two-body phase space. Initial unpolarized states are averaged; unobserved final polarizations are summed. An isotropic amplitude integrates to σ=(∣kf​∣/∣pi​∣)∣M∣2​/(16πs). A full-solid-angle integral for identical final particles additionally needs its symmetry factor.

Physics OurBigBook.com

A liquid that produces particle scintillation when deposited energy excites its components. Photomultipliers can convert the emitted light into detector pulses.

Physical law

Words: 52
Physics OurBigBook.com
A physical law expresses a reproducible relation used to describe or predict physical phenomena within its domain of applicability. Applying it requires a model specifying the system and conditions: Newton's second law, together with a force model, predicts a body's acceleration; conservation of energy constrains exchanges within a specified system. Its predictions must be compared with physical observations.

Gravity

Words: 94 Articles: 2
Physics OurBigBook.com
Gravity governs falling bodies and orbits. Newtonian gravity describes it through a gravitational field acting on masses; general relativity instead relates matter and radiation to the geometry of spacetime through the Einstein field equations.

Gravitational force (F=−m∇Φ)

Words: 26
Gravity OurBigBook.com
The force exerted through gravity. In a Newtonian gravitational potential Φ per unit mass, a point mass m experiences the displayed force, while a continuous mass density ρ experiences force density −ρ∇Φ.

Gravitational field (g)

Words: 43
Gravity OurBigBook.com
In Newtonian gravity, the gravitational field g specifies the acceleration of a freely falling test particle at each position. A gravitational potential Φ gives g=−∇Φ, with the gradient taken in the spatial geometry of the model. In general relativity, the metric tensor describes gravitational effects, and tidal forces are encoded by spacetime curvature.

Metrology

Words: 1k Articles: 92
Physics OurBigBook.com
Metrology asks what a measurement means and how closely it can be reproduced. An instrument reading becomes useful when it is related to a reference through measurement calibration, with a stated measurement uncertainty. Measuring a changing object against a changing ruler makes the problem especially clear: an observed difference contains the responses of both.

Dimensional metrology

Words: 525 Articles: 4
Metrology OurBigBook.com
Measurement of length and geometrical dimensions. A length standard supplies a reference; a differential length comparator measures the difference between two lengths rather than treating its own structure as perfectly invariant.

Length standard

Words: 22
Dimensional metrology OurBigBook.com
A reference realizing a specified length, under specified conditions. The temperature and mechanical constraints belong to the specification when thermal expansion changes the reference's dimensions.

Differential length comparator

Words: 308 Articles: 1
Dimensional metrology OurBigBook.com
An instrument for comparing two lengths through their difference. Suppose a test rod and reference both have length L0​ at temperature T0​, and have constant linear thermal expansion coefficients αs​ and αr​ over a small interval. Their first-order models give
Ls​(T)=L0​[1+αs​(T−T0​)],Lr​(T)=L0​[1+αr​(T−T0​)].
(1)
For the observed difference D(T)=Ls​(T)−Lr​(T), the derivative b=dD/dT therefore determines
αs​=αr​+L0​b​​.
(2)
The reference's independently calibrated linear thermal expansion coefficient is essential: the difference alone identifies αs​−αr​, not either coefficient separately.
For an original numerical example, stipulate L0​=1.00m, αs​=1.0×10−6K−1 and αr​=9.0×10−6K−1. Heating both by 10K gives sample and reference increases of 10μm and 90μm. Thus the sample expands even though its measured difference decreases by 80μm. These are chosen model parameters, not measured values for a historical Invar specimen or reference.
If αr​ and b have independent standard uncertainties 0.2×10−6K−1 and 0.3μmK−1, and uncertainty in L0​ is negligible, variance additivity for independent random variables gives
u(αs​)=u(αr​)2+L02​u(b)2​​≃0.36×10−6K−1.
(3)
Repeating the difference measurement can reduce its random contribution; it does not remove uncertainty in the reference. A temperature gradient or unequal rod temperatures also breaks the common-temperature model and can introduce a systematic error.
ABBA measurement sequence (B−A​=(y1​+y2​−y0​−y3​)/2)
Words: 121
Differential length comparator OurBigBook.com
Alternating sample and reference readings can suppress instrument drift. In this original four-reading model, measure objects A,B,B,A at equally spaced times 0,Δt,2Δt,3Δt. Assume the objects are stable during that short sequence and each reading is its object's length plus the same affine function of time, a+bt. Then
B−A​=2y1​+y2​−y0​−y3​​=LB​−LA​,
(4)
because both pairs have mean time 3Δt/2. The constant offset and linear drift cancel. With a further drift term ct2, direct substitution instead leaves bias −2cΔt2. A shorter sequence reduces that term, but neither this ordering nor averaging corrects unequal temperatures, sample changes or reference measurement uncertainty. This is a modern illustrative protocol; the historical account below establishes alternation, without attributing this particular four-reading sequence to Charles-Édouard Guillaume.

Guillaume thermal expansion experiment

Words: 170
Dimensional metrology OurBigBook.com
Charles-Édouard Guillaume sought affordable, stable length standards. His 1920 lecture describes two micrometer microscopes on stone supports sighting marks on a rod immersed in water. Their separation was not fixed: one method alternated the sample with a reference in a second trough at nearly constant temperature. His relative method compared sample and platinum–iridium reference in the same bath, adding the reference's known expansion to the measured difference. Composition and treatment affected the nickel–iron alloys; low expansion held over a limited temperature range.[ref]
The differential length comparator calculation explains why a calibrated reference is needed even when its expansion is larger than the sample's. Keeping both rods in the same bath targets one source of systematic error; allowing for changes in the instrument baseline targets another. Discovering a low-expansion alloy and demonstrating its dimensional stability are connected experimental tasks.

Metrology OurBigBook.com
A quantified spread of values attributable to a measured quantity, accounting for relevant measurement information and corrections.

Measurement uncertainty budget

Words: 49
Measurement uncertainty OurBigBook.com
A record of uncertainty contributions in a specified measurement model, their evaluation methods, sensitivity coefficients and relevant correlations. For y=g(x1​,…,xn​), first-order propagation of uncertainty gives uy2​=∑ij​(∂i​g)(∂j​g)Cov(xi​,xj​). A correction for a known systematic error can itself have uncertainty; applying the correction does not remove that contribution.[ref]

Systematic uncertainty

Words: 49
Systematic error OurBigBook.com
Uncertainty associated with imperfect knowledge of calibration, efficiency, backgrounds or other persistent model inputs. Repeating the same measurement does not necessarily average it away. Correlated nuisance parameters can propagate it through a likelihood; estimating such an uncertainty is distinct from asserting that the systematic error has a known sign and magnitude.

Common-offset cancellation by signal reversal (S=(y+​−y−​)/2,b=(y+​+y−​)/2)

Words: 56
Systematic error OurBigBook.com
If a controlled reversal changes the desired signal's sign while leaving an additive offset unchanged, readings y+​=S+b and y−​=−S+b separate them by half-difference and half-sum. Offset drift, gain changes, hysteresis or a background that also reverses violate the simple cancellation. Interleaving polarities and independent blank measurements test those assumptions; signal reversal does not cancel an arbitrary systematic error.

Systematic-error cancellation by reversal

Words: 73
Systematic error OurBigBook.com
If a wanted response changes sign on reversing a controlled setting while an offset remains unchanged, the difference of the reversed readings isolates the response. For V±​=±RI+V0​, the estimator (V+​−V−​)/(2I) cancels V0​. The method requires offset stability between readings. It does not cancel a common current-scale calibration error, and it does not remove even-in-current Joule heating. A useful reversal test specifies which physical effects change sign, then tests the remaining effects independently.

Measurement calibration

Metrology OurBigBook.com
Comparing an instrument indication with a reference of known value to establish their relation and its measurement uncertainty.

Words: 45
Measurement calibration OurBigBook.com
A constant additive contribution b to an instrument reading is a zero offset. A blank or zero-signal reading can estimate it, and a systematic-error cancellation by reversal can cancel it if it remains unchanged while the desired signal changes sign. The residual correction uncertainty remains part of the measurement uncertainty.

A change in an instrument's response or zero point with time. A reference measured alongside the target can track the component shared by reference and target light.

Pycnometer

Words: 22
Metrology OurBigBook.com
A calibrated vessel used to infer a liquid's mass density from its mass and filled volume; see pycnometer density measurement for an inspected experiment and the accounting formula.

Measurement resolution

Words: 38
Metrology OurBigBook.com
Measurement resolution is the smallest change in an instrument indication that its reading method can distinguish. It contributes to measurement uncertainty, but does not by itself establish accuracy or remove systematic error. The manometer height-to-pressure calibration shows how a height scale affects the inferred pressure.

Unit of measurement

Words: 124 Articles: 14
Metrology OurBigBook.com
A unit of measurement is a chosen reference for comparing magnitudes of a physical quantity. A value written as a number times a measurement unit changes its numerical part when the measurement unit changes, while representing the same physical quantity.

Plasma (physics)

Words: 2k Articles: 49
Physics OurBigBook.com
A plasma is a gas of mobile charged particles whose collective electromagnetic response is important to its dynamics. It commonly contains ions and electrons, and may also contain a neutral component: complete ionization is not required. A multi-species fluid description has current density J=∑s​qs​ns​us​. The relative motion of the species can matter even when a single-fluid magnetohydrodynamics approximation describes the large-scale dynamics.

Tokamak

Words: 96 Articles: 1
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
A toroidal magnetic-confinement system combining an externally imposed toroidal field with a poloidal field supplied largely by toroidal plasma current. The resulting helical field-line winding supports nested magnetic flux surfaces and improves orbit confinement compared with a purely toroidal field. Confinement remains limited by orbit effects, collisions and instabilities.

Tokamak safety factor (qs​≃rBϕ​/(R0​Bθ​))

Words: 50
Tokamak OurBigBook.com
A measure of toroidal field-line turns per poloidal turn. In the circular large-aspect-ratio approximation, geometry gives qs​≃rBϕ​/(R0​Bθ​). With Ampère's law, Bθ​(a)≃μ0​Ip​/(2πa), so the edge value relates the field-line pitch to the toroidal plasma current. This geometrical estimate alone does not establish stability for a complete current profile.

Inverse bremsstrahlung

Words: 38
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
Collisional absorption of electromagnetic wave energy by charged particles scattering from other charges. In a weakly collisional unmagnetized Drude model, with X=ωp2​/ω2<1, the intensity absorption coefficient is αI​≃(νei​/c)X/1−X​. The corresponding electric-field amplitude decays at half that rate.

Critical plasma density (nc​=ϵ0​me​ω02​/e2)

Words: 30
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
The electron density at which the cold unmagnetized electron plasma frequency equals an applied electromagnetic frequency. In the collisionless linear model, transverse radiation below this cutoff does not propagate in a uniform bulk plasma.

Coulomb logarithm (lnΛ)

Words: 29
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
The logarithm of the ratio of effective maximum to minimum impact parameter in weakly coupled Coulomb collision transport. Screening and short-distance scattering determine the cutoffs; it encodes many small-angle encounters.

Coulomb coupling (Γ=4πϵ0​akB​Te2​)

Words: 28
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
The importance of electrostatic interaction energy compared with thermal energy. For mean separation a, a common measure is Γ=e2/(4πϵ0​akB​T); the weakly coupled regime has Γ≪1.

Plasma parameter (ND​=34π​ne​λD3​)

Words: 24
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
The number of electrons in a Debye sphere, here ND​=(4π/3)ne​λD3​. A large value characterizes weak fluctuations and weak coupling in the ordinary collective-screening regime.

Stochastic heating

Words: 49
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
Increase of particle random kinetic energy due to decorrelating electromagnetic kicks. In the simple unscreened electrostatic white noise limit it is velocity-space diffusion with constant coefficient and heating rate mnD. In other plasma settings the same term can refer to orbit stochasticity produced by spatial structure or overlapping resonances; its precise mechanism must be stated.

Resonant heating

Words: 53
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
Transfer of fluctuation energy to particles selected by a wave-particle resonance. For a weakly damped Langmuir wave, particles near its phase velocity absorb net energy from a stable distribution by Landau damping. Under weak random forcing, a smaller damping rate produces a larger stationary wave intensity; a very long waiting time may be required before that stationary balance holds.

Ion-temperature-gradient instability (ITG)

Words: 41
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
A drift-scale plasma instability fed by an ion temperature gradient. In common electrostatic limits, Boltzmann electron response, ion temperature evolution, magnetic drifts and polarization drift determine the dynamics. Unfavorable magnetic field-line curvature can drive a toroidal branch; straight-field branches can involve parallel compression. The threshold depends on the equilibrium gradients and geometry.

Electrostatic plasma wave (δE=−ikϕ)

Words: 189 Articles: 3
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
A plasma wave dominated by a longitudinal electric field. The leading dispersion relation is k⋅ϵ⋅k=0. In a cold magnetized plasma, this becomes k⊥2​S+k∥2​P=0. An exactly longitudinal finite-wavenumber solution must also satisfy the full Maxwell equations; the oblique electrostatic condition is usually an asymptotic large-refractive index approximation.

Degenerate-plasma dielectric response (ϵ=1+k2vF2​3ωp2​​[1−2s​logs−1s+1​],s=kvF​ω​>1)

Words: 97 Articles: 1
Electrostatic plasma wave OurBigBook.com
For an isotropic completely degenerate nonrelativistic Fermi gas in classical-trajectory collisionless kinetic theory, the parallel marginal distribution is F(u)=3n(vF2​−u2)1∣u∣<vF​​/(4vF3​). Integrating F′(u)/(u−ω/k) yields the electron dielectric function in the title for fixed ions. Its real roots outside the occupied interval have no Landau damping. Quantum recoil, collisions and finite-temperature tails require an enlarged model.
Degenerate-plasma zero-point sound (ω=±kvF​(1+δ),δ∼2e−2−2k2vF2​/(3ωp2​))
Words: 51
Degenerate-plasma dielectric response OurBigBook.com
The short-wavelength root of the degenerate-plasma dielectric response, approaching the edge of the occupied parallel velocity interval from outside. Writing s=1+δ makes its logarithmic singularity give the exponentially small positive correction in the title. It is the high-wavenumber limit of the charged Langmuir wave branch in this approximation; neutral zero sound has a different interaction and long-wavelength limit.

Boltzmann electron response (δne​/n0e​=eϕ/Te​)

Words: 51
Electrostatic plasma wave OurBigBook.com
Rapid parallel thermal electron streaming can approximately balance electrostatic and isothermal pressure forces, giving ne​∝eeϕ/Te​ and its linear form in the title. This assumes a suitable connection along the magnetic field, ∣ω∣≪k∥​vth,e​, and an approximately electrostatic branch. A spatially constant potential on a closed line requires its own particle-number constraint.

Cold magnetized plasma

Words: 295 Articles: 7
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
A plasma whose linear wave response retains the equilibrium magnetic field and particle inertia but neglects pressure forces, thermal dispersion and collisions. Its applicability requires kvth,s​≪∣ω∣ and separate care near cyclotron resonances.

Plasma wave resonance (n2→∞)

Words: 39
Cold magnetized plasma OurBigBook.com
A limiting point of a plasma wave branch with divergent refractive index. At finite coefficients of the magnetized cold-plasma dielectric tensor, the generic condition is Ssin2θ+Pcos2θ=0. Poles of that magnetized cold-plasma dielectric tensor require a separate limiting analysis. Collisions, thermal dispersion or mode conversion can regularize a singular cold prediction.

Plasma wave cutoff (n2→0)

Words: 43
Cold magnetized plasma OurBigBook.com
A point on a plasma wave branch where the local wavenumber tends to zero at finite frequency. The mode may change between propagation and evanescence. For a finite magnetized cold-plasma dielectric tensor, candidate cutoffs satisfy PRL=0; special propagation angles require checking which factor belongs to the chosen branch.

Extraordinary plasma wave (n2=RL/S)

Words: 33
Cold magnetized plasma OurBigBook.com
For propagation perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field, this plasma wave has its electric field perpendicular to that magnetic field and generally both parallel and perpendicular to its wavevector. Its dispersion relation is n2=RL/S, using the magnetized cold-plasma dielectric tensor conventions R=S−g, L=S+g.

Ordinary plasma wave (n2=P)

Words: 40
Cold magnetized plasma OurBigBook.com
For propagation perpendicular to an equilibrium magnetic field, an ordinary plasma wave has its electric field parallel to that magnetic field, so the particle response involves no magnetic deflection. With immobile ions, the dispersion relation is ω2=ωpe2​+c2k2. It is a transverse electromagnetic wave, despite its parallel particle motion.

Cold-plasma left-handed wave (n2=L=S+g)

Words: 19
Cold magnetized plasma OurBigBook.com
With the same conventions as the cold-plasma right-handed wave, this transverse electromagnetic wave has Ey​=−iEx​ and refractive index n2=S+g. With immobile ions, L=1−ωpe2​/[ω(ω+Ωe​)].

Cold-plasma right-handed wave (n2=R=S−g)

Words: 36
Cold magnetized plasma OurBigBook.com
For propagation along +B0​, use eikz−iωt and ϵxy​=ig. This transverse electromagnetic wave has Ey​=iEx​ and refractive index n2=S−g. Its real electric field rotates in the sense of electron gyration. With immobile ions and positive electron cyclotron frequency magnitude Ωe​, R=1−ωpe2​/[ω(ω−Ωe​)].

Magnetized cold-plasma dielectric tensor (ϵ)

Words: 59
Cold magnetized plasma OurBigBook.com
For e−iωt, Gaussian units give ϵ=I+4πiσ/ω, where σ is the summed conductivity tensor. With the equilibrium magnetic field along z, write ϵxx​=ϵyy​=S, ϵzz​=P, and ϵxy​=−ϵyx​=ig. For signed cyclotron frequencies Ωs​=qs​B/(ms​c),
S=1−∑s​ω2−Ωs2​ωps2​​,P=1−∑s​ω2ωps2​​,g=−∑s​ω(ω2−Ωs2​)ωps2​Ωs​​.
(5)
Here ωps​ is the species plasma frequency. The two circular eigenvalues are S∓g; defining the sign convention before naming their polarizations prevents ambiguity.

Landau damping

Words: 348 Articles: 4
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
Collisionless damping of a collective plasma perturbation by phase mixing and resonant exchange with particles near its phase velocity. In linear electrostatic response, the imaginary part of the dielectric function at real frequency is proportional to the derivative of the equilibrium phase-space distribution function at resonance. A velocity plateau removes this contribution on an interval; compact velocity support also permits undamped waves whose phase velocities lie outside that support.

Collisionless phase mixing

Words: 62
Landau damping OurBigBook.com
For freely streaming particles, a spatial Fourier perturbation of a velocity distribution evolves with factors e−ikvt. Contributions from different velocities acquire different phases and can cancel in a density or field moment even while the fine-grained distribution retains structure. In a self-consistent plasma, resonant field–particle exchange gives Landau damping. This is distinct from collisional thermalization and from orbital phase mixing in a planetary ensemble.

Maxwellian beam threshold for a positive velocity slope (nb​/np​>e​Vσb2​σp−3​e−V2/(2σp2​))

Words: 91
Landau damping OurBigBook.com
A broad electron Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of width σp​ plus a narrow beam of width σb​ centred at speed V can have a positive resonant velocity slope. The beam slope is largest at V−σb​. Treating the background slope as constant over the beam width gives the displayed density threshold. Replacing the Maxwellian tail at V−σb​ by its value at V also requires Vσb​/σp2​≪1; width separation alone does not ensure that exponentially sensitive approximation. A positive slope is the local resonant-drive criterion, while an exact unstable mode also requires the kinetic dispersion relation.

Landau mode (ϵk​(ωj​)=0)

Words: 78
Landau damping OurBigBook.com
A pole of the causally continued collective kinetic response, usually a zero of its scalar response denominator or response-matrix determinant. With time dependence e−iωj​t, negative imaginary part gives damping, positive imaginary part growth, and zero imaginary part an undamped oscillation. Damped poles need not be regular discrete eigenmodes of the original collisionless operator: their contribution is obtained by continuing the initial-value response. The least damped excited pole can set the waiting time for a stationary forced response.

Landau contour (CL​)

Words: 60
Landau damping OurBigBook.com
The velocity-integration contour implementing causal continuation of a kinetic response from the upper complex phase velocity half-plane. As a pole approaches the real axis, the contour passes below it. With denominator v−u, the real-axis limit is PV∫f0′​(v)/(v−u)dv+iπf0′​(u). Continuing the pole below the axis keeps this causal prescription rather than simply replacing the contour by an undeformed real-axis integral.

Inductively coupled plasma

Words: 9
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
A plasma maintained by energy transfer from a time-varying magnetic field.

Quasineutrality (∑s​qs​ns​≃0)

Words: 56
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
On spatial scales much larger than the Debye length, a plasma may have nearly cancelling positive and negative electric charge densities while still carrying an electric current and having a nonzero electric field. Quasineutrality is an approximation on appropriate slow macroscopic scales, not an assertion that each fluid element has exactly zero charge or that charge separation can be ignored at every boundary.

Plasmon

Words: 429 Articles: 8
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
A plasmon is a quantum of a collective oscillation of electric charge density in a plasma or conducting material. Long-range Coulomb interaction can give its long-wavelength longitudinal mode a nonzero frequency.

Plasma oscillation

Words: 269 Articles: 5
Plasmon OurBigBook.com
A plasma oscillation is a collective oscillation of charge density and its restoring electric field. In a three-dimensional bulk charged superfluid, long-range Coulomb forces give the longitudinal collective mode a nonzero long-wave plasma frequency. Different geometry and electromagnetic boundary conditions can change that limit.
Ion-acoustic wave (ω≃kcs​)
Words: 110 Articles: 1
Plasma oscillation OurBigBook.com
A low-frequency electrostatic plasma wave with ion inertia and a pressure restoring force, usually dominated by electron pressure. Weak ion Landau damping requires the phase velocity to exceed typical ion speeds. Electron Landau damping depends on the electron parallel marginal distribution and need not vanish even when ion damping is absent.
Degenerate ion-acoustic wave (cs2​≃me​vFe2​/(3mi​))
Words: 68
Ion-acoustic wave OurBigBook.com
For equal densities of singly charged ions and electrons, a completely degenerate electron equation of state gives dPe​/dne​=me​vFe2​/3. Coupling this restoring force to ion inertia yields the sound speed in the title. If both species are degenerate and me​≪mi​, then vFi​≪cs​≪vFe​. Ion resonances are absent, while the electron parallel marginal distribution has a small slope at the phase velocity, producing relative Landau damping of order me​/mi​​.
Electron acoustic wave
Words: 52
Plasma oscillation OurBigBook.com
An electron-supported electrostatic branch with approximately linear small-wavenumber dispersion relation ω≃kua​. A velocity plateau can support such a completely undamped mode even when ion response is neglected. A single Maxwellian electron population generally damps the corresponding acoustic response strongly. Distinct electron populations provide another setting for electron acoustic behavior, with different assumptions and damping properties.
Langmuir wave
Words: 67 Articles: 1
Plasma oscillation OurBigBook.com
A longitudinal electron plasma oscillation whose long-wavelength frequency approaches the electron plasma frequency when ions can be treated as stationary. Its dispersion relation and Landau damping depend on the electron phase-space distribution function. Compact velocity support can permit exactly undamped branches outside the support.
Degenerate-plasma Langmuir dispersion (ω2=ωp2​+53​k2vF2​+O(k4))
Words: 34
Langmuir wave OurBigBook.com
The long-wavelength root of the degenerate-plasma dielectric response. Expanding its logarithm at large s=ω/(kvF​) gives ϵ=1−ωp2​/ω2−3ωp2​k2vF2​/(5ω4)+⋯. The occupied Fermi sphere has ⟨v∥2​⟩=vF2​/5, accounting for the dispersive coefficient. The static electron response instead defines the Thomas-Fermi screening length vF​/(3​ωp​).

Surface plasmon polariton

Words: 135 Articles: 1
Plasmon OurBigBook.com
A transverse magnetic polarization electromagnetic wave bound to an interface through coupling to the material's collective charge response. Its fields propagate along the interface and decay away from it on both sides. In an ideal nonmagnetic lossless planar vacuum-material interface, a real negative relative permittivity below −1 supports the bound branch described by the lossless planar surface-plasmon dispersion. Material losses generally make the propagation constant complex.
Lossless planar surface-plasmon dispersion (k2=(ω2/c2)ϵ/(ϵ+1))
Words: 78
Surface plasmon polariton OurBigBook.com
For a vacuum-material interface at z=0, write the magnetic phasor as Hy​eikx−βj​z, with β1​>0 in vacuum and β2​<0 in the material. The Ampere-Maxwell law gives Ex​=iβj​Hy​/(ωε0​ϵj​) and Ez​=−kHy​/(ωε0​ϵj​). Tangential field continuity gives β2​=ϵβ1​. Together with k2−βj2​=ϵj​ω2/c2, this gives the displayed relation and requires ϵ<−1 for real propagating k and decay on both sides. For ϵ=1−ωp2​/ω2, the branch has 0<ω<ωp​/2​ and approaches that upper frequency only as k→∞. At low frequency, k=(ω/c)[1+ω2/(2ωp2​)+O(ω4/ωp4​)].

Plasma screening

Words: 142 Articles: 3
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
Collective electric charge rearrangement modifies particle interactions in a plasma. In stellar nuclear fusion, this response can alter the Coulomb barrier used to infer a thermonuclear reaction rate.

Debye length (λD​=ϵ0​kB​Te​/(ne​e2)​)

Words: 122 Articles: 2
Plasma screening OurBigBook.com
For mobile thermal electrons with a fixed neutralizing background, the Debye length is the characteristic distance over which plasma screening suppresses an electrostatic perturbation. Linearizing the Boltzmann density response and using Poisson's equation gives the displayed scale. Other mobile species contribute additively to λD−2​ through ns​qs2​/(ϵ0​kB​Ts​).
Debye sphere
Words: 79 Articles: 1
Debye length OurBigBook.com
A sphere of radius equal to the Debye length. Its particle count defines one common normalization of the plasma parameter.
Number of electrons in a Debye sphere from a plasmon energy ratio (ND​=82​/(9πr3))
Words: 61
Debye sphere OurBigBook.com
For a three-dimensional ideal degenerate electron gas, let r=ℏωpe​/EF​. If one heuristically defines a Debye length by replacing kB​T with the Fermi energy, then kF​λD​=2​/r and the associated electron count is the displayed expression. A count below one signals failure of the classical many-particle screening interpretation. It does not prohibit plasmons. The zero-temperature compressibility instead gives the Thomas-Fermi screening length squared 2ϵ0​EF​/(3ne​e2).

Plasma frequency (ωps​=ns​qs2​/(ϵ0​ms​)​)

Words: 255 Articles: 5
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
The plasma frequency is the characteristic electrostatic oscillation frequency of a charged species displaced against a neutralizing background. For number density ns​, charge qs​ and mass ms​, the displayed formula uses SI units; in Gaussian units it is ωps​=4πns​qs2​/ms​​. The ion skin depth is c/ωpi​ for the ion species. Different species have different plasma frequencies.

Transverse wave cutoff in a cold unmagnetized plasma

Words: 33 Articles: 1
Plasma frequency OurBigBook.com
With immobile ions, negligible collisions and electron density ne​, the plasma frequency is ωp2​=ne​e2/(me​ϵ0​). Combining inertial electron current with vacuum displacement current gives ω2=ωp2​+c2k2. Transverse fields are evanescent below ωp​ and propagate above it.
Carrier-current double counting in effective permittivity
Transverse wave cutoff in a cold unmagnetized plasma OurBigBook.com

Cold collisionless plasma dielectric response (εr​=1−ωp2​/ω2)

Words: 168 Articles: 2
Plasma frequency OurBigBook.com
In an unmagnetized plasma, an electron displacement driven by Ee−iωt obeys −me​ω2xe​=−eE. Its dipole moment is −exe​, giving electric polarization P=−ne2E/(me​ω2). With D=ε0​E+P, this yields the displayed relative permittivity and ωp2​=ne2/(me​ε0​). Ions contribute a further negative term smaller by Zme​/mi​ for one ion species of charge Ze. Neglecting it requires heavy ions at electron-wave frequencies; collisions, background magnetization and pressure dispersion are excluded. The transverse electromagnetic wave relation is c2k2=ω2−ωp2​.
Inferring incident power from a transmitted plasma field
Words: 58
Cold collisionless plasma dielectric response OurBigBook.com
For a downward transverse wave in an isotropic plasma, Ez​/Ex​=tanθt​ fixes the transmitted direction. Tangential phase matching gives sinθi​=np​sinθt​. Continuity of tangential electric and magnetic fields then separates incident and reflected amplitudes. A measured transmitted electric amplitude alone cannot be identified with the incident one; mean power for peak phasors includes a factor of one half, and interface-normal flux includes a cosine.

Philosophy of physics studies the interpretation and explanatory structure of physical theories, including the relation between mathematical models, observable phenomena and claims about what exists. Its questions include theoretical reduction, emergence and competing formulations of physical locality.

Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
The material variables that a physical theory identifies with the distribution of stuff in ordinary space or spacetime, and through which it describes apparatus and recorded events. In particle Bohmian mechanics, actual particle configurations play this role; the wave function guides them. This is a way to specify an interpretation's account of matter, rather than a theorem that only particle ontologies are admissible.[ref]

Constructive theory

Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
An account that builds macroscopic processes from specified constituent systems and their interactions. Kinetic theory explaining thermal behavior through molecular motion is a standard example. A constructive theory and a principle theory can address the same phenomena at different explanatory levels.[ref]

Principle theory

Words: 39
Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
A physical theory organized around general empirical constraints on admissible processes, rather than a specified microscopic mechanism. Albert Einstein used thermodynamics and special relativity as examples. This classification concerns the explanatory strategy; a principle theory can constrain possible constructive theories.[ref]

Stochastic Einstein locality

Words: 65
Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
A formulation of stochastic Einstein locality restricts an event's objective chance to its relevant causal past, rather than spacelike-separated interventions or facts. Different versions constrain either marginal chances or joint conditional probabilities. A one-wing marginal condition alone does not supply outcome independence. To derive a Bell theorem by this route, the proposed locality assumptions must include the appropriate screening-off relation for the two outcomes, together with a common setting-independent past distribution.

Reichenbach common cause principle

Words: 76
Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
A classical common-cause explanation seeks past variables which screen off a correlation: conditioned on a sufficiently complete common cause, the correlated events become independent. A Bell local causality model adds local dependence on settings and a single compatible past-variable distribution for all measurement contexts. Providing a different setting-dependent screening variable for each pair of settings does not establish that stronger Bell model. The distinction between a causal mechanism and a purely probabilistic screening construction matters when interpreting this principle.

Emergence

Words: 57
Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
Emergence concerns novel collective patterns or explanatory structures relative to a lower-level description. Robust effective behaviour can emerge through coarse-graining or singular limits while remaining derivable from the microscopic theory. The stronger claim that genuinely new causal powers cannot be reduced to that theory requires an additional argument; nonanalyticity of a limiting function alone does not establish it.

Theoretical reduction

Words: 55
Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
Theoretical reduction relates theories by deriving the laws or predictions of one from another together with explicit identifications of quantities and appropriate domain assumptions. A reduction can require approximation, coarse-graining or a limiting construction. Deduction of an ideal limiting model is different from exact deduction of the same properties for every finite member of a model sequence.

A nuclide formed in or descended from nuclear fission. The inventory includes unstable species and their decay products and evolves with irradiation and elapsed time.

Nuclear fission OurBigBook.com
A sequence in which particles released by one nuclear reaction induce further reactions. In a neutron-driven fission chain, neutron capture, leakage and non-fission absorption compete with neutron production. A sustained chain requires an effective reproduction factor of one; whether material is fissile material cannot be determined from a single positive fission Q value.

Words: 31
Nuclear fission OurBigBook.com
Material convertible into a fissile material by neutron capture followed by nuclear transformations. A central example is uranium-238 capturing a neutron and undergoing two beta-minus decays to plutonium-239. Fertile does not mean that thermal-neutron capture immediately causes fission.

Fissile material

Words: 41
Nuclear fission OurBigBook.com
Material capable of sustaining a nuclear chain reaction with slow neutrons in a suitable configuration. Fissility involves capture and fission probabilities, neutron production and losses, rather than positive fission Q value alone. Uranium-235 and plutonium-239 are common examples; fissile is more specific than fissionable by sufficiently energetic neutrons.

Words: 56
Nuclear fission OurBigBook.com
In a simple compound-nucleus picture, compare the neutron-capture excitation energy to the fission barrier of the capture product. If its neutron separation energy already exceeds the barrier, slow-neutron capture can lead to prompt fission without a positive kinetic-energy threshold. If it lies below, finite neutron kinetic energy is needed for appreciable over-barrier fission; sub-barrier tunnelling and detailed resonance widths soften a literal sharp-threshold picture.

Fission-fragment mass distribution

Words: 65
Nuclear fission OurBigBook.com
The yield of fragments as a function of fragment mass number or mass fraction. Low-excitation actinide nuclear fission commonly gives two peaks, corresponding to complementary lighter and heavier fragments. Smooth liquid-drop fission energy by itself does not predict this yield: nuclear-shell structure and the dynamics of the descent toward scission matter. Increasing excitation can weaken shell effects and change the distribution. A two-peaked illustrative curve is therefore not a universal measured spectrum.

Spontaneous fission

Words: 42
Nuclear fission OurBigBook.com
Nuclear fission without an incoming particle supplying the activation energy. A metastable atomic nucleus can tunnel through a fission barrier along collective deformation coordinates. The rate depends exponentially on a barrier action involving its height, width and collective inertia, so positive liquid-drop fission energy alone does not imply an observable rate.

Fission barrier

Words: 61
Nuclear fission OurBigBook.com
The increase in a nucleus's collective deformation potential energy between a local minimum and a saddle on a path toward separated fragments. A positive final-state Q value does not remove this intermediate barrier. A nucleus can cross it after sufficient excitation energy, or undergo quantum tunnelling. The relevant barrier for neutron-induced fission belongs to the compound nucleus formed after capture, not automatically to the target before capture.

In the semi-empirical mass formula without nuclear pairing, nucleon rest energies, the volume term and the nuclear symmetry energy cancel in the parent-minus-fragment mass difference. The remaining Q value is the displayed competition between increased surface energy and reduced nuclear Coulomb energy. Its symmetric value is positive when
AZ2​>aC​aS​​1−2−2/321/3−1​.
(8)
This is an energy-release condition, not the disappearance of a fission barrier or a prediction of a short mean lifetime.

Ignore nuclear pairing and use the continuous proportional-fragment model of liquid-drop fission energy. Put S=aS​A2/3, x=aC​Z2/(aS​A) and t=y1/3+(1−y)1/3. As y runs from zero to 1/2, t rises from 1 to 22/3. The identity u3+v3=1 with u=y1/3 and v=(1−y)1/3 gives
SQ​=1+x−3t2+2/t​+9x​(t5−5t2−5/t),dtd(Q/S)​=9t2t3−1​[5x(t3−1)−6].

The derivative changes sign at most once, from negative to positive. Thus the global maximum on the closed continuous interval occurs at either the no-split endpoint Q=0 or the symmetric split. If positive fission energy is available, the symmetric value is the global maximum. This qualification matters: symmetry alone makes y=1/2 stationary but does not make it a maximum for all parameters. In fact, Q′′(1/2)<0 requires Z2/A>(2/5)aS​/aC​; below that value the symmetric split is a local minimum. Real discrete fragments and nuclear-shell corrections are outside this continuous smooth model.

Radioactive decay (N(t)=N0​e−λt)

Words: 4k Articles: 61
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
Radioactive decay is the spontaneous transformation of an unstable atomic nucleus or nuclear state. Its timing can be unpredictable for an individual atomic nucleus while a large population has a reproducible average behavior. A constant nuclear decay constant λ>0 gives the familiar exponential decay law. The half-life describes how quickly the parent population falls, while radioactive activity describes its rate of transformations.[ref]
This connection between randomness and a regular population law makes radioactive decay useful for measuring elapsed time and for understanding sources of radiogenic heating. It also distinguishes two questions in an experiment: what the source emits, and what an instrument records. Becquerel's uranium-radiation experiment used a photographic plate; the Curie ionization-current measurement measured an electrical consequence of radiation. Their readouts reveal different aspects of the same investigation.

Thus ratios of excitation energies inferred from line separations do not need the common recoil factor. The nuclear states must obey ∣Ji​−Jf​∣≤J≤Ji​+Jf​, and their parities satisfy πf​/πi​=(−1)l in this leading orbital classification. The least permitted l labels the degree of forbiddenness. The original functional diagram separates the two signal mechanisms and their timing. It omits dimensions and phototube counts, and is not a reproduction of a historical drawing. The measured objects are detector pulses; identifying their common cause also requires calibration and background tests.

Diluting the target with heavy water halved the proton density and reactor signal while preserving neutron-detection efficiency. In his 2 March 1896 report, Henri Becquerel described uranium salt crystals acting on a photographic plate through opaque wrapping. A copper cross weakened the exposure behind it. Ordinary baryons have three valence quarks, and ordinary mesons have a quark and an antiquark. Additive quantum numbers such as electric charge, baryon number and strangeness are sums of constituent values. The quark model makes a large catalogue manageable: the same few quark flavors generate many different hadrons. It predicts relations between electric charge, strangeness and isospin, rather than assigning these independently to each new particle. It is especially useful for asking which combinations are possible and which additional measurements could distinguish them. A constituent list alone does not determine a mass, a decay rate or whether a proposed combination forms a bound state.

An antiquark reverses all five displayed values. These are flavor coordinates, not spatial coordinates or electroweak hypercharge.

Likewise, the neutral pion flavor direction (uuˉ−ddˉ)/2​ and the Eta octet state (uuˉ+ddˉ−2ssˉ)/6​ both have Q=Y=0, but their inner product vanishes. Expanding that inner product gives (1−1+0)/12​=0. (25)
These formulas follow directly from the constituent table. With fixed ns​, there are 4−ns​ possible values of nu​, so the weight diagram has rows of four, three, two and one states. Its outer triangle is therefore a consequence of the constituent construction, rather than an arbitrary drawing convention.
The bottom corner has ns​=3, hence I3​=0, Y=−2 and Q=−1: the Omega baryon position. The top-right corner has uuu and Q=2, corresponding to the doubly charged Delta baryon. Every point satisfies the Gell-Mann--Nishijima formula Q=I3​+Y/2.
The flavor construction is only part of the state. The Pauli constraint on three-quark flavour multiplets also involves spin angular momentum, the spatial wavefunction and color charge. In particular, three identical fermions cannot be assigned a completely symmetric total state merely because the flavor diagram is symmetric. Nor does the same flavor diagram determine the hadron masses: an approximate flavor symmetry can organize a spectrum without making all its members degenerate.

George Zweig's 1964 CERN model used three constituents called aces, with fractional electric charge and baryon number 1/3. Omega baryon discovery experiment
Words: 201
Omega baryon OurBigBook.com
The 1964 report exposed Brookhaven's 80-inch hydrogen bubble chamber to a mass-separated 5.0GeV/c negative-kaon beam. A photographed decay chain, track momenta and bubble density supported the particle identification. Two converted photons helped reconstruct a neutral pion. Alternative assignments were tested kinematically. The authors reported an Omega baryon candidate with Q=−1, S=−3 and mass 1686±12MeV/c2, reserving a detailed systematic-error discussion for further events.[ref]
This is an inference from several linked observations. A charged particle can leave a visible bubble-chamber track, while a neutral segment must be reconstructed from its production and decay products. Agreement between possible decay channels, electric charge, momentum conservation and the reconstructed mass is stronger evidence than a suggestive track shape alone. The event tests a predicted hadron pattern; it does not photograph the three strange quarks individually.
For example, an independently constructed two-body kinematic check uses
M2c4=(E1​+E2​)2−c2∣p1​+p2​∣2.
(27)
In a parent rest frame with equal and opposite daughter momenta, the momentum sum vanishes, giving Mc2=E1​+E2​. In units c=1, stipulated daughter masses m1​=1, m2​=1/4 and momentum magnitude p=3/4 give E1​=5/4, E2​=10​/4 and M=(5+10​)/4≃2.04057. A common Lorentz boost changes the daughter energies and momenta while preserving this reconstructed invariant mass. These chosen units and numbers are an illustration, not a reanalysis of the 1964 event.

Molecular beam

Words: 942 Articles: 7
Experimental apparatus OurBigBook.com
A directed stream of molecules used to prepare samples for spectroscopy.
A molecular beam also includes a stream of chemical atoms, then called an atomic beam. An oven supplies particles; aligned slits restrict their directions, and a vacuum limits subsequent collisions. Narrowing the directions does not by itself make every particle's speed equal. This gives a useful separation of tasks: prepare a path, select or measure speed, apply an interaction, and read the resulting particle counts or deflection.
The advantage is unusually tangible. A magnetic field can separate spin components in the Stern-Gerlach experiment; even gravity can sort a beam by flight time. The effusive beam speed distribution explains which particles leave the source, while gravity deflection of an atomic beam explains how that distribution becomes a pattern on a detector.

Dunoyer molecular-beam experiment

Words: 68
Molecular beam OurBigBook.com
In 1911, Louis Dunoyer de Segonzac formed a sodium beam in vacuum and collected a deposit on a surface cooled with liquid air. Its shape agreed with straight paths through the slits.[ref] A deposit tests the geometry of the surviving paths. A clock or a calibrated deflection is needed to turn their travel into a speed measurement.

Effusive beam speed distribution (g(v)=vf(v)/⟨v⟩)

Words: 192
Molecular beam OurBigBook.com
Which speed distribution does an arrival counter measure? Suppose an equilibrium, nonrelativistic ideal gas escapes by effusion through a thin opening into vacuum. The opening is small compared with the mean free path; the reservoir remains at temperature T. Let f(v) denote its normalized Maxwell speed distribution, with mass m and a=m/(2kB​T):
f(v)=π​4a3/2​v2e−av2,v>0.
(28)
At a given direction toward the opening, the number crossing per unit time is proportional to the normal component vcosθ. Integrating over a fixed accepted cone contributes an angular factor independent of v. Thus the normalized probability density function for speeds among arriving particles is
g(v)=⟨v⟩vf(v)​=2a2v3e−av2​.
(29)
Its integral is one because ∫0∞​v3e−av2dv=1/(2a2). The reservoir mode is v=2kB​T/m​; the arrival mode is 3kB​T/m​. Faster particles get more opportunities to cross the opening. This is a selection effect, not heating after emission.
Specify the observable before applying the formula. An instantaneous count in a fixed segment of the beam weights the arrival flux by the time spent there, proportional to 1/v; in this ideal model its normalized speed law returns to f(v). A detector's speed-dependent efficiency, source collisions or a velocity selector changes the arriving law again. Counting arrivals and counting particles currently present are different measurements.

Rotating-wheel molecular velocity selector

Words: 167
Molecular beam OurBigBook.com
Otto Stern's lecture describes two co-rotating toothed wheels: transit between them must match an advance between openings. He explicitly distinguishes this method from the first historical speed measurement.[ref]
For an idealized example, let aligned wheels have N equally spaced openings, separation L, and rotation rate f in revolutions per second. A particle with constant longitudinal speed v takes L/v between them. The second wheel advances through fL/v revolutions; transmission peaks when that advance is an integer number k of opening pitches:
vk​=kNfL​​,k=1,2,….
(30)
With chosen N=60, f=50Hz and L=0.080m, the first two orders select 240 and 120ms−1. A second transmission maximum therefore need not represent a second source temperature. Finite opening widths admit speed intervals around each order, and an additional measurement is needed to distinguish orders. The ideal expression assumes negligible acceleration and constant rotation rate during a flight, with a fixed relative phase between the wheels.

Gravity deflection of an atomic beam (y=gL2/(2v2))

Words: 358
Molecular beam OurBigBook.com
Immanuel Estermann, O. C. Simpson and Otto Stern used gravitational deflection to measure atomic speeds. Stern describes scanning a hot-wire surface ionization detector through a cesium beam and recording ion electric current.[ref] Their 1947 paper reports potassium and cesium beams; a deficit of slow arrivals increased with oven pressure, supporting a source-slit collision explanation.[ref]
First consider an original point-launch model, with horizontal speed v>0, zero initial vertical velocity, flight distance L, and uniform gravitational acceleration g. Downward displacement y follows from flight time t=L/v:
y=2v2gL2​=v2C​,C=2gL2​.
(31)
Slow particles fall farther. However, a detector scan counts arrivals per interval of height, not per interval of speed. Change of variables for probability densities supplies the Jacobian determinant:
py​(y)=g(C/y​)2y3/2C​​=y3b2​e−b/y,b=aC=4kB​TmgL2​,y>0.
(32)
Here g(v) denotes the effusive beam speed distribution; the unadorned constant g in C denotes gravitational acceleration. The integral of py​ is one: substituting u=b/y reduces it to ∫0∞​ue−udu=1. Its mode is y=b/3. Simply mapping the most probable arrival speed into a fall distance instead gives 2b/3. The peaks differ because equal height bins cover unequal speed intervals.
For those chosen parameters, b≃176.54μm, so the detector-height probability density peaks near 58.85μm. A detector covering only 0<y<Y accepts the fraction
F(Y)=∫0Y​py​(y)dy=e−b/Y(1+Yb​).
(33)
At Y=0.80mm this is about 97.9%, even before allowing for imperfect detection. Discarding the remainder changes the observed normalization.
Real slits transmit a range of launch heights and vertical velocities. Their geometrical response must be combined with the gravitational deflection and detector width; the point-launch formula is not an exact reduction of the historical apparatus. In the point-launch model, an initial vertical velocity w would add wL/v to y. Source collisions, detector efficiency and alignment can also distort a profile. Varying oven pressure helps distinguish such source losses from an incorrect thermal distribution; inferring a source temperature from the peak alone ignores both selection and the detector's coordinate transformation.

A discovery becomes more intelligible when its motivating question, proposed explanation and actual measurement can be followed together. The photoelectric effect connects Albert Einstein's light-quantum reasoning with the Millikan photoelectric experiment. The Schrödinger equation and the Davisson–Germer experiment connect mathematical wave mechanics with a laboratory test of matter waves.
The Nobel Prize in Physics provides one route through these subjects. Following the original papers and the people who built the apparatus also brings collaborators into view: Lester Halbert Germer appears alongside Clinton J. Davisson in the Davisson–Germer experiment. The history belongs in the articles on those people and concepts as well as in award records.

A periodic modulation of electronic charge density, often coupled to a lattice distortion. In a one-dimensional metal, a Peierls distortion with Q=2kF​ can open a gap at opposite Fermi points, lowering the occupied electron energy at an elastic energy cost. A charge modulation and a spin density wave are distinct: the latter can modulate spin while leaving the total charge nearly uniform.

Spin density wave (S(x)=S0​cos(Qx+φ))

Words: 26
Condensed matter physics OurBigBook.com
A spatially modulated spin density, distinct from a charge density wave. Opposite modulations of spin-up and spin-down occupations can give a periodically varying magnetization while their total charge density stays uniform.

Electron correlation

Words: 433 Articles: 10
Condensed matter physics OurBigBook.com
Electron-gas correlation energy
Words: 37
Electron correlation OurBigBook.com
The exact ground-state energy minus the minimum Hartree-Fock energy for the same Hamiltonian and variational constraints. It is nonpositive when compared with the unrestricted variational minimum. Correlations beyond a single determinant can substantially change phase boundaries at low density.
Dissociation error of a doubly occupied bonding orbital
Words: 47
Electron correlation OurBigBook.com
A normalized product of two identical bonding orbitals built from separated orthogonal centers has finite weight in configurations with both electrons on one center. Repulsion penalizes that ionic weight even when hopping disappears. Mixing configurations can instead approach one electron per center while preserving the required spin and exchange symmetries.
Dynamic electron correlation
Words: 34
Electron correlation OurBigBook.com
The correlated instantaneous avoidance of electrons beyond a single Slater determinant. It can remain important even when one configuration dominates, as for an isolated closed-shell helium atom; it is distinct from the near-degeneracy problem of static electron correlation.
Static electron correlation
Words: 36
Electron correlation OurBigBook.com
Electron correlation caused by the need for multiple important configurations, often when several molecular orbitals are nearly degenerate. Stretching a homonuclear two-electron bond makes a single doubly occupied orbital retain unphysical ionic contributions; a suitable combination of configurations cancels them.
Heavy fermion material
Words: 164 Articles: 2
Electron correlation OurBigBook.com
A strongly correlated material whose low-energy electronic quasiparticles have a very large thermodynamic effective mass. An enhanced electronic heat capacity coefficient, spin susceptibility and quantum-oscillation cyclotron effective mass are complementary signatures; they need not all be related by a single isotropic band mass. A Kondo lattice is an important setting for such behaviour. In CeAl3, low-temperature specific heat and quadratic resistivity provided an early quantitative example.[ref]
Electronic heat capacity of a heavy Fermi liquid
Words: 34
Heavy fermion material OurBigBook.com
For quasiparticles with density of states g(EF​) including both spins, the leading electronic heat capacity is C=γT with γ=π2kB2​g(EF​)/3. A narrow heavy band makes this coefficient large. The density of states and heat capacity must use consistent extensive, molar or volumetric normalization.
Low-temperature calorimetry and resistivity of CeAl3
Words: 66
Heavy fermion material OurBigBook.com
The 1975 measurements of CeAl3 below 0.2K found an electronic heat capacity coefficient of 1.62Jmol−1K−2 and a quadratic electrical-resistivity coefficient of 35μΩcmK−2. These are complementary thermal and transport signatures of an unusually dense low-energy electronic spectrum.[ref] A temperature sweep and a C/T versus T2 fit separate the electronic intercept from a Debye lattice term; the transport comparison tests a Fermi liquid temperature law.
Kondo effect
Words: 115 Articles: 2
Electron correlation OurBigBook.com
Antiferromagnetic exchange between a localized magnetic moment and conduction electrons produces strong low-energy correlations and screening of the moment. In a dilute magnetic-impurity metal, a resistance minimum and a low-temperature logarithmic increase are characteristic signatures over an appropriate temperature range. The strong-coupling low-temperature regime cannot be obtained by extending the logarithm indefinitely.
Kondo lattice
Words: 64 Articles: 1
Kondo effect OurBigBook.com
A periodic array of local moments coupled to conduction electrons. Competition between screening, coherent hybridization and intersite magnetic interactions can produce a heavy fermion material, magnetic order or a correlated insulating state.
Kondo-lattice coherence temperature
Words: 34
Kondo lattice OurBigBook.com
A Kondo lattice develops coherent low-energy quasiparticle bands below a material-dependent coherence scale. This lattice scale need not equal the single-impurity Kondo screening scale. Coherence can produce a heavy Fermi liquid with narrow bands, large electronic heat capacity and low-temperature quadratic resistivity.

Soft matter

Words: 100 Articles: 2
Branches of physics OurBigBook.com
Soft matter studies materials whose large-scale structures respond strongly to modest mechanical or thermal disturbances, including polymers, liquid crystals and colloids. Polymer physics connects chain conformations to material response; the coil-stretch transition is one example.

Synthetic fluid membrane

Words: 59
Soft matter OurBigBook.com
A synthetic fluid membrane is a thin self-assembled sheet of synthetic amphiphiles, fluid under static in-plane shear while resisting area changes and bending. It provides a nonbiological realization of a two-dimensional fluid interface with curvature elasticity. A Helfrich energy describes long-wavelength shape costs; its material parameters and any spontaneous curvature depend on composition and conditions. Lateral fluidity does not eliminate membrane bending rigidity or membrane tension. The membrane fluctuation spectrum under tension separates bending-dominated and tension-dominated length scales.

Soft matter physics

Words: 14
Soft matter OurBigBook.com
Soft matter physics studies the physical behaviour of soft matter, including its response to mechanical and thermal perturbations.

The study of physical properties and processes in the oceans, including fluid flow, waves and transport of heat.

El Niño–Southern Oscillation

Words: 69 Articles: 2
Physical oceanography OurBigBook.com
Coupled variability of the tropical Pacific ocean and terrestrial atmosphere, including the warm El Niño phase, the cold La Niña phase, and associated changes in surface pressure, trade winds and the thermocline.
La Niña
Words: 13
El Niño–Southern Oscillation OurBigBook.com
The cold phase of El Niño–Southern Oscillation, with central and eastern equatorial Pacific surface cooling.
El Niño
Words: 31
El Niño–Southern Oscillation OurBigBook.com
The warm phase of the coupled tropical Pacific El Niño–Southern Oscillation, with central and eastern equatorial Pacific surface warming and a weakened Walker circulation. Changes of trade winds, thermocline depth, and equatorial Kelvin waves and equatorial Rossby waves participate in its evolution.

Thermocline

Words: 46
Physical oceanography OurBigBook.com
A water layer across which temperature changes rapidly with depth. In a reduced gravity description of the upper ocean, its displacement is represented by the interface between warm surface water and colder deep water. Deepening the eastern tropical Pacific thermocline makes upwelling less effective at cooling the surface during El Niño.

Scalar particle (J=0)

Words: 35
Particle (physics) OurBigBook.com
A scalar particle has zero intrinsic spin. A scalar-field excitation provides its relativistic description. Spin zero alone does not force its decay matrix element to be independent of internal invariant masses; resonance dynamics can still produce a nonuniform three-body distribution.

Massless particle (pμpμ​=0)

Words: 29
Particle (physics) OurBigBook.com
A particle with zero invariant rest mass. A positive-energy massless state has E=∣p∣ in natural units and has no rest frame. Its finite-helicity representations differ from massive spin representations.

Massive particle

Words: 21
Particle (physics) OurBigBook.com
A particle with strictly positive rest mass. Its relativistic energy obeys E2=p2c2+m2c4, and its speed in an inertial frame is below the speed of light.

Neutral particle

Words: 5
Particle (physics) OurBigBook.com
A particle with zero net electric charge.

Particle number (N)

Words: 90 Articles: 1
Particle (physics) OurBigBook.com
A particle number counts the particles of a specified kind in a system. For a fixed collection, N is a nonnegative integer. In a variable-number quantum system, distinguish a measured particle number, the particle number operator, and its expected value.

Particle current (JN​=−dNL​/dt)

Words: 58
Particle number OurBigBook.com
The rate at which particles cross an oriented surface, measured as particle count per unit time. If a local continuity equation has number density n and current density jN​, then ∂t​n+∇⋅jN​=0 and JN​=∫S​jN​⋅dS. In a closed two-reservoir system, a left-to-right particle current is −dNL​/dt=dNR​/dt. Neutral particles carry this current without an associated electric current.
